title: Don Quixote and the Windmills
text:
Don Quixote, a country gentleman who had read so many tales of chivalry that he believed himself a knight errant, rode out across the plains of La Mancha with his squire, Sancho Panza. As they went, they came in sight of thirty or forty windmills standing on the plain.

Don Quixote's eyes lit up. Fortune, he declared, was guiding them better than they could have wished. There before them were monstrous giants, and he meant to fight them all and take their spoils. Defeating them would be a service to God.

Sancho asked what giants he meant. Those over there, said the knight, with the long arms. Sancho pointed out that they were windmills, and what looked like arms were their sails, which turned in the wind and drove the millstones.

Don Quixote replied that Sancho clearly knew nothing of adventures, and if he was afraid, he could stand aside and pray. Then he spurred his horse, Rocinante, and charged at the nearest windmill, lance leveled. Just then the wind rose and the sails began to turn. His lance pierced a sail, which swung up and shattered it, and flung horse and rider rolling across the field.

Sancho found him badly bruised. Even then, Don Quixote insisted that an enchanter had turned the giants into windmills to rob him of his victory.
lesson: Check that the enemy you are charging is real. If everyone around you sees a windmill, at least pause before you lower your lance.
source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part I, Chapter 8
